utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Today we're here for the Kvocka case. Good morning to the interpreters, to the technicians. We will be sitting here, the two of us, Judge Wald and myself, without Judge Riad at the beginning. He will arrive around 11.00. We apologise to all of the participants in the courtroom for this delay. Again we had certain organisational problems, and we are trying to work on it, and we hope that this will not happen again. So today we will continue with the testimony of Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kvocka. As you know, you are still under oath. I would like to ask Mr. Simic how long does he think that he needs to finish the testimony of Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I hope that I will be able to complete the evidence today, in any event, and that there will probably be time for Mr. Radic to take the stand. I think that we will use most of the day today, anyway, in order to complete our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm asking because, as you know, pursuant to Article 15 of the Statute, if the Chamber cannot sit in full composition, the Judges may decide to continue, and we think that it is in the interests of justice to continue even in the absence of Judge Riad. As I have already told you, he will be here around 11.00, and we'll have a break around that time. So I think that we can work now until 11.10 or 11.15, and then we will have a break and we will come back with Judge Riad. Mr. Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, after you returned from Tukovi, what did you do? What were your duties in the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: After I came back from the reserve police station in Tukovi, I was a policeman at the duty room in the Prijedor police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you describe what your duties were and how did you go about carrying them out?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In the Prijedor police station, I worked as a policeman, as a part of the duty service. This is a group of five or six men who were part of this duty service. There is a shift commander, there is a driver, and several police officers for different calls and other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in this job?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: For about a year. Until I was transferred to the Chief of Patrol in the Prijedor Police Station I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Sometime in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender another exhibit now. Our mark is 27. My apologies again, but we will place this exhibit on the ELMO, and this way we will avoid any confusion with different markings.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D22/1, and D22/1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, what was established in early August in the Prijedor police station, according to this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In the public security station in Prijedor, in early August, a police battalion was established consisting of seven companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of this battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In which company were you, which platoon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I was a member of the 1st Company and the 1st Platoon of this company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was your platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was Milorad Marin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was the company commander?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Milutin Cadjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, how many superior persons were there if you take the entire structure into account, the companies and platoons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Including the command, that is, the command staff and the company and platoon commanders, there are about 63 different commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When you look at the proportion of the command staff in relation to the entire staff of the security station in Omarska --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You mean Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, actually, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I believe that at the time, there were somewhere between 160 and 170 active-duty police officers in the public security station in Prijedor, and one could conclude that every third active-duty police officer was one of the commanding officers whom I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When you look at the list of these commanders, their deputies, and so on, what was their function in the regular police force, apart from this battalion structure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The top officials of the public security station were involved there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was Staff Commander Simo Drljaca; and Deputy Commander was Marko Djenadija, Reserve 1st Class Captain; and then Chief of Staff was Dusan Jankovic, who was also the head of the police department; and the operative officer was Ranko Mijic, who was a Reserve Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I just want to take you back to the 1st Company. What was the commander of the 1st Company within the overall Prijedor police structure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Milutin Cadjo, at that time, was also the commander of the Prijedor I Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, several days ago you talked about certain changes when you came back from that vacation which you took after the incident. What changes did you observe in the system of organisation of the Omarska Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: After I came back from this leave, I think I have mentioned certain changes, and even earlier, there were some minor changes. On the very same day that the incident which I described took place, that is, the shooting of that individual and my intervention and the death of one or two detainees, which was on the 31st of May, before all this had happened, Zeljko was away, and after his return, he was both angry and concerned. He said that there were more serious tasks ahead and that he had to do something in order to improve the efficiency of the police work in the Omarska police station. In that sense, he said that he would organise the police work into three shifts and that there would be a duty officer assigned to each of the shifts, and that he has been considering these things and that Mladjo Radic, as an experienced police officer, was definitely going to be among them. He also was familiar with radio communications. And he was still labouring about finding the other two because he said that he didn't have the right choices for those two positions. Then perhaps supported by my suggestions, he said that perhaps Milojica Kos and Momcilo Gruban, called Ckalja, could be those two choices. They projected the image of fairly stable police officers, and they were very straightforward. And this is what he actually ended up doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How did he let Kos and Gruban know that they were appointed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think when they arrived at the station, he told them that these would be their assignments, that they would be also manning the radio transmitter and that occasionally they should note down if somebody failed to appear for work. He told me that this would also be good for me because I was burdened and that this would help, because at that time, I had duty shifts of 12 hours each day. When I said that he had asked me to work in this way, in the previous days, when I say "asked," it was really an order because we did not have regular strict orders, but when they said, "Please do such and such a thing," the order was implicit in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you are a long-time police officer, and later on you advanced in your career. What was this position? Was this some kind of a commanding post?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You mean the duty officer's duty?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: By rank, that was a position that was like any other position, something that any other police officer would have done either in the investigation centre or in the police department, it's the same thing. The only difference is the tasks that you get.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let us try to simplify this. Could Mr. Radic have issued any orders to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you have issued any orders to Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Radic have issued orders to any reserve police officers in the shift where he was on duty?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who could issue orders to whom? We're talking about security staff.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Only Zeljko Meakic could issue any types of orders to either myself or Radic or any other police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, were you present at any incident after this short leave which you took after the shooting incident in the Omarska Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were several situations after my return from my leave, things that I observed, and in some, I took part, and I can enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In the first days, on this plateaux in front of these buildings, a person appeared who was known to the police officers in Omarska before as a criminal type. That was Vlado Sredic, called Djordjin. He was armed, he was obviously inebriated, and very loudly, he cursed Turkish mothers, and he was yelling something to the effect, "Where is the hodza from Kevljani so that I can try him," and similar things. When I heard this, I walked over to him and rather curtly, and actually somewhat forcefully, removed him from the centre. He left the investigation centre mumbling something, saying something to the effect that "We are catching them, and here you are treating them with silk gloves." Then later on, an acquaintance of mine from the traffic police told me that he had met this same Djordjin person at the checkpoint where he worked, that he openly issued threats that I was the first on the list of people with whom he was going to deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any additional incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In that same period, I had two incidents at the front gate. When I was on duty in the office which we most frequently used as the duty room, I received a call by this internal phone from the front gate that the police officers and the company guard had certain problems with drunken individuals who wanted to enter the investigation centre. After I received this information and request for assistance, which is how I would define it, I immediately set out for the front gate and found four soldiers, armed, who had arrived in a vehicle. They were drunken also and they wanted to come in, and they were demanding that the gate be opened by the company guard. The gate was opened automatically from the guard's hut, and I tried, using my experience in similar situations, to calm things down and to convince them to leave there, because any other approach would have been quite risky. They were all armed and quite aggressive. From the previous era, which was the Communist system, as they called it, they had inherited this arrogant attitude towards the policemen. They asked me why I was protecting the Turks and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned "Turks," in the previous incident where this single person called them Turks and now they call these people Turks. What was this word used for?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was a derogatory word for the Muslims who lived in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: After several such exchanges, they decided to leave after all, again mumbling something under their breath and making noises, but I paid no more attention to them and I went back to the building. And speaking of incidents, I can also mention an incident which took place around 10 June, when in the morning I found Zeljko Meakic, and in conversation with him learned that in the course of that night, a murder had taken place. Mehmedalija Nasic, I believe. I know that the last name is Nasic. He briefly described that during the night a guard had shot through the window of the restaurant where the detainees were staying, that apparently he had been trying to flee or something, and that the guard named Popovic or Pavlovic had used the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You were not in Omarska that night?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I was not on duty that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the police officer who had shot? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I only know that this policeman was off duty for five or six days, but later on he reappeared. I saw him in his guard post, if I can call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any measures were taken against him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any other incidents which you observed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: During my stay there, which was a total of about 20 days, I observed several people who had bruises, which means that they had received beatings. I also observed, during one arrest of about seven or eight persons, an official vehicle which had come from Prijedor, it was a police van, that a search was conducted of these individuals, and I think that it was done not in a correct way. It was humiliating. But if you think that -- but a police search can be construed to feel humiliating anyway, but this one was out of the ordinary. I said, "Boys, this is not how this should be done. It should be done properly." I think then that the search from there on went properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, it is not our task to identify all the personnel in the police force, but what was the ethnic composition of the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any other police officers by the name of Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were two additional ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: One was Zoran, one was Milojica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When we talked about the structure of security and you said that you only controlled one point -- I'm not going to go back to that -- but there was one point that I think that we need to clarify. Concerning the police officers who were sort of servicing the investigators, who was their superior?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was Zeljko Meakic as the commander of the police precinct, but they were attached to the investigators, and they received orders from the investigators as to whom they were to bring forth, and that's, in a nutshell, how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did your brothers-in-law stay in Omarska after you departed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I mean when they arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: After they came, they stayed in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I mean after they went back to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I brought them back to the investigation centre somewhere around the 22nd, 23rd, and they stayed there until the Omarska centre was closed down. That was in early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where were they taken then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were all taken to Trnopolje, all three.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When were they released from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were released from Trnopolje several days later. Up to one week later after they were transferred from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who went to get them in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were released in such a way that my wife and I went there in the vehicle and brought them home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they receive any help before you arrived back to your place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: When we came there, we found some Red Cross personnel who drafted a document saying that they could leave, but somebody objected, said that these signatures were not enough. The signature of Slobodan Kuruzovic was needed for it, but he refused to give us his signature. We then decided to take them into the vehicle and leave anyway and see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you have any trouble getting to or from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There is a checkpoint as you exit, and our documents were checked there. They noted down our information. I was quite crudely provoked there, because they asked why am I releasing the Green Berets. What did I think I was doing. There were five or six men at this checkpoint. They were armed. I think that one of them even cursed my mother. I was humiliated, to sum it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, let us go back to the indictment now. Who was responsible for hygiene, the prisoners' hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: According to the document that we studied a few days ago, it was the mine administration, the strip mine administration; that is to say, the company administration. It was up to them to organise them. I noticed two or three individuals, two or three females, women, whom I knew previously to be cleaners in the company compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask us to look at a document, D17/1, point 7 on page 2 of this document. Our number is 55. The document is numbered 55, to facilitate communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I shall read this out: "At the same time, the mine's management is duty-bound to do regular cleaning, maintenance of plumbing, electrical fixtures and other utilities. It shall also ensure other kinds of logistical support of the work and stay of the given number of persons on the given premises by imposing obligatory work on skilled employees as is stated in the document." In practice did it function that way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were a number of individuals. Some of them I knew worked in the compound earlier on, and they were in charge of keeping the premises clean, as you stipulated a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The members of the police station of Omarska, did they have anybody amongst them to see to the hygienic conditions in the compound?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How did the members of the department -- how could they influence the sanitary conditions and improve them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they were able to do so at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: This brings us to a number of individuals and a figure is mentioned. I would like to ask you for some information about that. How many detainees were there in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I would say that there were between two to two and a half thousand detainees. So between 2.000 and 2.500 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the department have an exact record of the number of people detained?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there the possibility of reconstructing this number by looking at how the food was distributed amongst the detainees? How was food distributed, actually?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The food was distributed throughout the day practically, from 10.00 in the morning up until 5.00 in the afternoon, 1700.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So in one group -- how many people would go to eat in one group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I think about 30 per time, because that was the number of people who could be catered for in the canteen, sit down in the canteen to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did it take for each meal to be eaten, for the dishes to be washed, and to get things ready for the second group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, as there were a lot of detainees, we had to speed up all these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to reconstruct and get at how many detainees there were. So how much time was necessary for one group of 30 detainees to be replaced by another group of 30 to have their meals and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: An assessment. Well, I have to resort to mathematics, but a maximum time span would be, let us say, five minutes. Five minutes was how long it took to serve one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the washing of dishes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The washing of dishes would also last several minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So shall we put an outside limit at, say, ten minutes? Can we say ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: If it is ten minutes per group, how many groups to one hour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, that would mean, if it's ten minutes for one group or one shift, then six shifts of this kind in one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And 30 people. How many would that make it per hour? How many people per hour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That would make it between 180 to 200 individuals per hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did this food distribution go on for? You said that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I said that it went on from about 10.00 in the morning, half past 9.00 sometimes, to 1700.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that, does your assessment of the number of detainees coincide with the mathematics we have just used?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, judging by these calculations, then it means that not everybody would have time to be served with food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was responsible for the food?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If you mean in the canteen itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: No, generally speaking. I mean food preparation and so on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the food was prepared in one main restaurant, in one main kitchen, which was located near the entrance gate. I think I mentioned this central kitchen earlier on, the central kitchen which catered for the mine compound. I think that there was some sort of chief cook there, and that his name was Pero Rendic. The person in charge of supplies, food supplies, as far as I know, was somebody called Milan Andzic, who was, at the same time, a logistics person in a sort of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who distributed the food in the canteen itself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, the food was distributed in the canteen by Zoran Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He belonged to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Since we're on the topic of food, who ate the food that was distributed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The food was eaten by all the detainees, and it was accessible by the guards as well. Some guards would eat there on some days, not on others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the investigators? What did they eat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The investigators were also given food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where did their food come from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Their food came from the same kitchen, but their food would be taken up to them on the floor on which they were, the larger premises, the larger office up on the storey. When they made a break, they would have lunch there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How many meals were the detainees given over a 24-hour period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: During the time that I was there, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what was each meal composed of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The meal consisted of -- that is to say, there was a plate of cooked food and a quarter of a loaf of bread. That was all they were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was it difficult to have bread supplies? Were there any upsets there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think that on one or two occasions there was a shortage of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The reason given, Pero Rendic would explain this when he would bring the inspectors their food, that he was having trouble with the work of the bakers because there were power cuts frequently, and so there were other problems of a technical nature in the baking of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: So who would bake the bread for the compound when this went on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you were an eyewitness of the sanitary conditions in the compound and the food supply, et cetera. Were the sanitary conditions in Omarska satisfactory, that is to say, were they commensurate to man, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I don't think they were, that is to say, they weren't. I say "I think," but in my view, they were below an acceptable level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the food?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't think the food was satisfactory either. The very fact that there was only one meal a day, and at that, the quality of the food wasn't very good, it was on a minimum level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This same document, Your Honour, is on the ELMO, and I would like to refer back to paragraph 7. It is document D55, Defence Exhibit 17/1; page 2, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I'd like to ask you to read the first sentence of paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't got the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then I'll read it out. It states as follows: "The Mine's management shall organise meals for investigators, guards, and detainees, according to norms established in agreement with the quartermaster service." Is that how meals were, in fact, organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the police department of the Omarska police station have any influence at all on the method and quality of the meals?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In this sense, no. Some of the guards, and this was something that we noticed, could bring somebody a sandwich, for example, or share his own sandwich with some of the detainees that they happened to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm asking, officially speaking, was there any possibility of you influencing the meals regime or organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, the indictment speaks of inadequate health protection, so I'd like to discuss that topic for a moment. Was there any form of organised health care in the investigation centre of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: With regard to health care, something did exist, yes, but the details as to how this was organised, I do not know. All I can say is what I myself saw and noticed, and that was that I noticed very often a paramedic called Ljuban Andzic from Omarska. He would spend some time in the Omarska Investigation Centre; he would bring some medicines and distribute them to some of the detainees. He contacted the detainees, this paramedic. I also noticed that on two occasions during my stay there a doctor from the health centre of Omarska, that is to say, it was a lady doctor, I remember that very well, she came and she put up a table on the grass over there [indicates], and together with a nurse, a line of detainees formed and one by one they went up to the doctor and the nurse and the table and they had some consultations with regard to their health. Another thing that I noticed was that in the investigation centre, on several occasions during my stay there, Dr. Ivic would turn up from Prijedor, he would visit, and he would come together with a paramedic, and his name was Mico or Mica. He was a paramedic without one arm, and I remember him. And that is what I noticed with regard to health care.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were there any doctors amongst the detainees themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There were several doctors -- rumour had it that there were several doctors amongst the detainees, but I knew one of them. I don't think he knew me very well but I did know him. I recognised him because he worked in the hospital at Prijedor previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: His name was Esad Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The people that came to the investigation centre of Omarska, did they contact the doctors who were in prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Ljuban Andzic did, I know about him, I know that he contacted a doctor. And on one occasion, Dr. Sadikovic personally asked me to try to bring him, if I could, all kinds of medicines, the medicines that I could come by, and other medical things, instruments, that he needed, and I did this because I would go to the Omarska health centre and ask the doctor on duty there to give me some medicaments and alcohol and bandages and things like that, which I then took to Dr. Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Ivic? Was Mr. Ivic of any service to you? Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivic, when he visited, would come by the office in which the police officers on duty were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you who had sent him, who was sending him to offer his services at the investigation centre of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, we would chat, because I knew him from Prijedor as being a doctor in Prijedor, and he would often say -- and he was bitter about it and he said, "How come they found me, in particular? How come Simo Drljaca picked me out of a whole hospital of doctors to come and visit the camp?" So those were the terms in which he spoke about all that, when we chatted. Otherwise, Dr. Ivic helped me in a certain -- one respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to tender a new exhibit. It has not been given a number. It is our number 47, the document that we have numbered 47. You will all be given a copy of the document, including the registrar, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be marked as Exhibit D23/1; D23/1A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What kind of help did Mr. Ivic provide you with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: On my left foot, I had some problems with my left foot, I had corns and also an ingrown toenail on my foot. I have suffered from an ingrown toenail since I was a boy. At the time, our footwear, we wore heavy footwear for long periods of time, and this was so sore that I could barely put my shoe on. So on one occasion, I think it was sometime in mid June, Ivic told me, that is to say, in that office, duty office, he cleaned this sore that I had, and he said that the only thing that could help me was not to wear shoes at all for several days, to let the sore clear up and calm down. On that occasion, he wrote a sick-leave certificate --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And how much leave did you get on the basis of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He gave me three days' leave, sick-leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the commander, Mr. Meakic, the station commander, about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander was present when all this was taking place, so he saw it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he give you sick-leave, a certificate for sick-leave?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The commander, Zeljko, said there would be no problems, and he told me to keep my sick-leave certificate, but that I was to complete one of my tasks in the police department in a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was all that about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, he said, "You'll probably be able to do that going in a car, so you won't need to wear a boot," and actually, it was -- I had to go to a woman named Desa Stanojevic. Before the war, she was well-known for taking money illegally, and before the war, the policemen from Omarska took away some of the money she had intended to smuggle. She engaged in contraband. So in the meantime, with the developments in Prijedor and all the things that were taking place, the money that had been seized from this woman was located in the police station, police department in Omarska. But Zeljko told me that the husband of this particular woman had been killed several days prior to that and that that money that had been seized ought to be returned to her because she had costs incurred over his burial and his funeral, and so on, and in situations of that kind, families, people had a lot of problems to pay for funerals because funerals are always expensive. So that was my assignment, and in the course of those three days, that is what I did, I found this woman and the money was returned to her, and that's where the whole case ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the husband's name, Mrs. Desa's husband's name, the husband who was killed? So that we can present the Trial Chamber with his name. Do you recall what his name was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. His name was Strahilo Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And when did you go back to work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I went back to work on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to another topic in the indictment, raised by the indictment -- and perhaps we will be able to complete by 11.15, Your Honours -- and that is the question of the contacts between the detainees and their families, their family members. Those contacts were forbidden. Zeljko's daily meetings with the policemen, he would say this to the policemen during his daily meetings with them. He stressed that all contacts between detainees and family members were prohibited. He said that there should be no contact either between policemen and the detainees. Mr. Kvocka, did anybody inform the family members of a detainee that a member of their family had been taken prisoner, where they were located and how they could be contacted, which is a fundamental right of all detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Officially, nobody did this, nobody informed them. I think it was difficult in practical terms. Possibly along private channels, somebody might have slipped some information to some family members, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: When you say not officially, what do you mean? Do you mean the department?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: And what about the security station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I should like once again to take another look at document D17/1, which is Defence Exhibit 55, that same document. Page 3, paragraph 15 this time. Mr. Kvocka, paragraph 15 of this key document relating to the organisation of the investigation centre, what does paragraph 15 state?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It says in this paragraph as follows: "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the public security station of Prijedor. This shall be the responsibility of the security staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there was an absolute ban on any kind of contact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the department or the staff of the police in Omarska, could they in any way whatsoever change the situation and enable people to have contacts and to alleviate and improve the very difficult detention conditions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The policemen had absolutely no influence. They could do absolutely nothing along the lines in which you have just spoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the abuse of this order. Were there any contacts, via the security staff, between detainees and their family members, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, if anybody did this, they would have violated or abused this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The conveyance of information, was any information brought into the detention centre by the guards?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I mentioned a moment ago that some of the guards would share their sandwiches with some people they knew, some of the detainees they knew. I personally did not take heed of the order strictly, and I would almost daily, when I came to work, practically every day when I came on duty, I would bring with me a whole carload of packages and different bags with food and clothing, and most frequently this -- what would happen was this: People knew that -- when I wasn't in my flat, people would come and leave packages in front of my front door, with the names of people to whom these bags should be distributed. And my mother-in-law as well, quite simply spent all her time collecting packages of this kind. It was a sort of collection centre, if I can call it that. Then everything that she had collected and had been left there I would take with me in my car and pass it round to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us some of the names of the detainees to whom you had taken packages of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, many of the people that I took packages to I didn't actually know personally, but the ones that I can remember, I can remember a few of the individuals that I had previously known, and one of those was Burazerovic, and he was nicknamed Braco, and he lived in my own apartment building, as did his wife and son, and they would bring me packages to take to their father every day. Another man's name was Suljo, I don't know his surname, but he also lived in my apartment building. He would bring packages for me to take to his brother. Mostly they were packages of food. And my mother-in-law, on several occasions, would prepare food herself for Mrs. Nusreta Sivac, whom she heard had been detained at the centre. As I have already said, my mother-in-law comes from an old Muslim family. I think that they knew each other very well from before and that my mother-in-law had a great deal of respect for that woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you take any packages to your colleagues at work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, I would share anything I had with my colleagues. One particularly interesting event was when the wife of Hamdija Arifagic found me in the Omarska settlement and asked me to take some food and clothing to her husband. I remember that meeting in particular because it was a very emotional one. Our two families, my family and his family, had been great friends before the war. We would go off on picnics together and things of that kind, so that that was a very emotional meeting with his wife, and tears were shed on both sides, may I add. I would take all these packages to Hamdija and have a brief conversation with him on the occasion. I know that there was some comments from some reserve policemen. They said why I didn't look at the loaf that I was taking, because there was a very big loaf that I took, and some of the policemen felt that there might be some weapons in the loaf of bread, but I just waved them aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, was that a good friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we were friends, and he worked together with me at Omarska before the events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he survived Omarska at all? Did he ever leave Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I never had any exact information, reliable information as to what happened to him, whether he was alive or not, but I haven't heard about him since. On several occasions after the investigation centre was disbanded, I had telephone calls in my flat from his brother. This man introduced himself as his brother. He appealed to me to collect any information I could about his brother, about Hamdija. However, on one occasion when I wasn't in my flat, my wife told me that she thought he was drunk when he called my wife, and he was rather vulgar on the occasion and spoke to her in very angry terms. Since then, we haven't had any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we have wound up that topic, and it is time for a break, as the Judge said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. Simic. We shall have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Fouad Riad hasn't arrived yet, so we are going to continue in the same composition and for the same reasons that we have announced. Maybe he will be back after the second break. At any rate, Mr. Simic, you may go on, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, throughout your time in Omarska, were there any other units that were in charge of providing security?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. At the very beginning, I believe for about two days, policemen from the Rakelici reserve police station came to Omarska as some kind of help, because of an insufficient number of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this happened on two occasions. They would come to work for one shift only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who was their commander? I mean, the commander of that police station.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was Milutin Bujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of the policemen who participated in that kind of assistance, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I know two of them, Ratko Kecan and Dusko Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, let us turn to the last issue of the examination; namely, the issue of visitors to the investigation centre of Omarska. While you were there in Omarska, were there any official visits to the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: While I was in Omarska, no, there were no official visits to the centre. I mean, no officials ever visited the camp. All I could observe was maybe Simo Drljaca coming to the investigation centre on two occasions, and on one occasion, I believe it was Dusan Jankovic who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise as to the date of their visits?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you with any certainty. It was sometime in the middle of my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who did they contact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Simo Drljaca went to see the investigators, the inspectors or team leaders who worked in the office that I mentioned some time ago. They were simply passing by us policemen. Once, I happened to be at the entrance of the administration building when Simo Drljaca was there, and he asked about Zeljko Meakic and went to the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any ceremony provided for for such visits, visits from the people from the Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. No, they came unannounced, as a surprise. They did not contact us at all, aside from saying hello to the people who happened to be standing nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: In addition to the, let us call them, officials, persons who came to visit the centre in their official capacity, were there any individuals coming to the centre who did not have that status?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, there was nobody else coming to visit the centre, except for those individuals who wanted to enter the centre without any authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had exactly that in mind. Were there any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I already told you about them, and that is all I know about such unauthorised visits, individuals getting in or attempting to get in, people who would come to the gate, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How was the control organised of such entrances? I'm referring to the security personnel. What type of control did they have?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As regards the access to the centre and entrances to the centre, I think that their work was very difficult. They did not have enough control. There would be a policeman at the gate, together with a workman from the mine, so these two people would be at the gate, and further on, there were some military personnel, a military checkpoint that you had to pass in order to reach the policemen who would stand at the entrance to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The Omarska police station and their personnel, were they in charge of providing security around the centre of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was the real influence of the public security station personnel? What was their ability to prevent unauthorised personnel from entering the Omarska centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The ability of the personnel to stop such individuals was actually very poor because anyone could reach the area of the investigation centre without being previously checked by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You have a long working experience as a policeman. Could you tell us about the number of people working in one shift? I have your police station in mind. What was the usual number of such people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There would be around 20 people per shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was that an adequate number of personnel for this number of buildings, premises, in order to provide appropriate security for the number of detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That was by no means enough, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Who could increase the number of personnel?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic could. He could perhaps request help from his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: But as regards the department itself, did he have enough personnel?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What was he supposed to do then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, he was probably supposed to contact his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any coordination between the security personnel, I mean the police department in charge of security, and the outside security personnel which was provided by the military?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In my opinion, as far as I could observe, there was no coordination whatsoever. Whether something was discussed, agreed upon at some other level, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could any of the soldiers from the military unit in charge of security have access to the centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: There were no obstacles for that whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, were there any women in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: While I was there -- it's very difficult for me to remember the exact number, but I should say there were about 15 women, but it well may have been 18 or 13. Maybe up to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: During the day they would be in the restaurant of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: During the night?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, they went to sleep on the upper floor of the administration building. They had maybe two or three offices for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were their living conditions compared to the living conditions of other detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I believe that their living conditions were somewhat better. I mean, they had something to sleep on. They had some kind of mattresses over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did they have access to toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. They had access to toilet facilities on a daily basis. They could use the toilet and a bathroom located in the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You have mentioned the issue of water. Was the water that was available there used by everybody, both guards and detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was. I used to drink it from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was the access to water denied to detainees? Were there any rations of water?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said that the water was available in the administration building. Was there any water on the pista?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the administration building, looking from my position here, on the side there was a kind of pump, a kind of fountain with several taps of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you say how many taps of water were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember exactly how many taps were there, but I believe that there were about five or six fountains that could be used at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: From both sides or from one side only?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I think that they were on both sides, but it's also possible that there was a line of -- there was several taps on one side only. It's very difficult for me to remember such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards water facilities in the hangar, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there was water in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: The security personnel, that is, the commander of the police station in charge of security, did he have any possibility to change the situation concerning water?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't think there was anything he could do in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you kill anyone in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, never. Not in Omarska, not ever in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you advise anyone, did you encourage anyone to kill anyone in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, never, and I would never do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you present during the incident that took place on the 31st? Were you present at any incident of a killing or murder?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever order anyone to kill?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I never did such a thing, nor would I ever do it, regardless of my position or the superior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. "Even if I had a position of a superior."

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever beat anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever help anyone beat anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever encourage anyone to beat?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present during a beating?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I was never present without intervening, and I think I have already spoken about such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: We have a model of the Omarska complex in front of us. Did you ever enter any of the buildings that you can see on the model of the Omarska compound?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did enter the building, the administration building, and I would spend some time there. As regards other buildings, I think I could have entered them. There would be no problems with my entering such building, but I didn't, except for the hangar when I had to order food and clothes. As regards the case involving Arif Omeragic [phoen], that took place in the hangar. But to be perfectly honest, I really avoided going there because during the food distribution, for example, I really felt that those people expected some kind of help from me, but I was perfectly aware that I was not in a position to help them. So I avoided entering those buildings, except when I had to deliver a package.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the White House?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the Red House?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards the female detainees, there were a few women who were familiar to you, whom you knew?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did any of them ever contact you? Did anyone ever complain about sexual assaults?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As regards the female detainees, I never had any such contacts. That issue was not mentioned. I was approached, for example, on a couple of occasions for a cigarette or in order to transmit a message to their relatives in Prijedor and so on. So those were the subjects of my conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate as to how many nights you were on duty in the Omarska Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: During my entire time there, I don't think I spent more than five nights in the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the premises, of the offices used by the female detainees, where were they exactly located?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: They were at the same corridor where the police unit had their premises, across the corridor from the office used by the duty police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, during your night shifts, did you ever observe any entries into the rooms that were occupied by female detainees?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. Such a thing never happened during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, why were you forced to leave Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I was made to leave, I believe, for several reasons, but they were not officially told -- I was never officially told about them, or unofficially, for that matter. But I think that the basic reason was the fact that I had violated certain rules; namely, because I took out my brothers-in-law without any authorisation; also because I brought in parcels and I tried to organise cigarette purchases, which I haven't mentioned yet. But once, upon the request of a detainee, I did that, and I was told not to do it again. So one can say that I had a conflict with investigators. I didn't think it was a serious conflict at the time; however, later on it turned out that it was more serious than I expected. So I believe that those were the basic reasons of my transfer. I know that people spoke about me and about my reasons for leaving, but that was the basic reason why I was transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was there any unusual event in relation to your departure from Omarska that took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Momcilo Gruban, nicknamed Ckalja, once told me about an incident. I visited my brothers-in-law maybe a week after my arrival to the centre, and Momcilo Gruban, on that occasion, told me that there had been a hunger strike attempt by detainees some time ago because, as they said, of my departure, because I had left. So Momcilo Gruban tried to convince them not to do it, even because of me, because it could have been interpreted in a negative way, and it could only cause me more trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said that after you left Omarska, you visited the centre -- you visited your brothers-in-law. On how many occasions did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Maybe on two or three occasions. The first one took place during the following week, and then there was one more, or maybe even two, I cannot remember, that took place during the ten following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: As regards your first visit to the centre, is there anything significant that -- was there anything significant that took place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: As regards my first visit to the centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I mean, did you see anyone beaten up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: On my first visit, I observed the first Serb who was detained there, his name was Igor Kondic, and I noticed that he had been severely beaten. He was detained in the same area as my brothers-in-law, and that's how I saw him. So he came to me and he asked me to try and get him one litre of mineral water, which I did, together with Zivko Puzac, who was a guard there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were the injuries of Mr. Kondic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: According to what I could tell, they were very severe. He had wounds all over his body. He only had a shirt on, so I could see that he was severely beaten up everywhere, on his head, on his arms, everywhere on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where is he from, Mr. Kondic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: He is from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he survived the wounding, the injuries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I heard later on that he had died in the Banja Luka hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: My last question for you. Mr. Kvocka, as a man, as a policeman, did you do everything that was in your power, that you could do, in those difficult times?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I honestly believe that I did everything I could, maybe even more, in view of the situation that I found myself in, that I did a lot to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my examination of Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before the witness is allowed to step down, we have two matters we would like to address. The first is, it has appeared to us that during the testimony the witness has had notes that he has used in his testimony. This is certainly unusual, in my experience, for a witness to have those. The Prosecution would like the opportunity to have a copy of those, or at least to review those notes. That's the first matter. The second matter is that perhaps this is the appropriate time to determine what the sequence of cross-examination will be, because I know the Prosecution has given its position that it wants to cross-examine at a later time. I don't believe that the other counsel for the other accused have given their position as to cross-examination and when they would like to do that. So perhaps that could be discussed and resolved at this time as well. And also, while we're at that, the order in which the cross-examination would occur. It's the Prosecution's position, because we have the burden in this case, that we would be the last to conduct cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. There are three questions here, the first one being the notes that were used by Mr. Kvocka, the second one is the one we are going to discuss, and the third one is the order of examination of the witness. I would like to hear the position of the Defence. Mr. Simic, as regards the first question, and two other questions as well -- I would also like to hear other Defence counsel as regards the second and third question -- but Mr. Simic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as notes are concerned, these are private notes of Mr. Kvocka. It is to be expected that if somebody is to be examined for three or four days, it is impossible to keep everything in mind. This is normal, to keep the notes. I am prepared to hand over two notes in which he reminds me to ask him the question about the applause, and then when the detainees leave. There was also an incident, to relay Mrs. Greve's remark about his reliability as a policeman. I think that these notes are incontrovertible. We have otherwise accepted the position of the Prosecution that the Prosecution should cross-examine the witness when they consider it the best for their case, and Mr. Niemann has stated that he would do that after all the Prosecution witnesses have given evidence. We have not addressed the issue of when the other counsel for the other accused would cross-examine Mr. Kvocka, we have simply not talked about it. I think that it could be done at the same time or in the same period when the Prosecution conducts its cross-examination, and I think that it is a matter for different Defence teams to agree on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, we do have to bear in mind the order. What is going to happen now, Mr. Simic, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Chamber's permission, if counsel for the other accused would like to cross-examine Mr. Kvocka now, I have nothing against this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Nikolic, let us hear you about the order of cross-examination. Could you state your position as regards that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence counsel for Mr. Kos would not examine Mr. Kvocka now. As far as the sequence is concerned, I believe that we have agreed that the Prosecution will cross-examine Mr. Kvocka after the presentation of evidence of their witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, Mr. Niemann requested to cross-examine first Mr. Kvocka and then Mr. Radic after completing their case-in-chief this is what was agreed on by us as well, and I see no problem in that. It is at that time that the Defence counsel of other accused will also cross-examine. So we understand that Mr. Kvocka has completed his examination-in-chief now, and then at the end of the Prosecution case-in-chief the cross-examination of Mr. Kvocka by the other Defence counsel will take place, followed by the Prosecution. This is my understanding, as far as I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour I completely second the positions of Mr. Simic, Mr. Fila. We are in complete agreement regarding the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We have already decided that at the end of the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kvocka, that there would be examination-in-chief of Mr. Radic. The Prosecution will be given an opportunity to cross-examine after completing their case. I don't know whether we have answered the question asked by Ms. Hollis. Maybe you had other issues in mind, other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Mr. Fila has answered the question that we had about the order of cross-examination. My understanding of what he said is that at the conclusion of our case, the other Defence counsel will cross-examine the accused who have testified, and then after they have completed their cross-examination, we will conduct our examination. That was the question that I had, what would be the exact order. So I believe that has been answered. Thank you. The only other matter outstanding, of course, is the decision about the notes. And just to clarify, Your Honour, perhaps I misunderstood Defence counsel for Mr. Kvocka. The Prosecution does not seek any access to notes that may have been passed by the accused to his counsel. We believe that that is confidential work product. What we are talking about were notes that it appeared the accused had before him as he testified, not notes that were passed to his counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I was clear. It is a regular thing for Mr. Kvocka to have had notes for the testimony, which is difficult testimony for a very difficult period of his time. I only wanted to illustrate what kind of notes Mr. Kvocka has made. I think that he should not be required to produce the notes which served him for his preparation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to consult with my colleague Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, there is a certain doubt that is here. I thought I understood that you would not ask questions, that is, that there would be no problems for the Prosecutor to see the notes, to have the notes. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was talking in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm referring to the notes that were used by Mr. Kvocka during his examination. I thought that you said that the Prosecutor can see the notes, that you see no problem about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the notes, and Mr. Kvocka has some additional notes that he has there. I think I need to consult with my client, because I myself do not know what is in those notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I think that Ms. Hollis has drawn attention to an important difference. There are notes that were exchanged between Mr. Kvocka and you. That's a thing apart. There is something else. The notes that were used by Mr. Kvocka during the testimony, I thought I understood that you said that you see no problem with the Prosecutor seeing, having access to the notes used by Mr. Kvocka during his testimony, and I would like to make sure that I have properly understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Notes in front of Mr. Kvocka are of the same nature. Those are confidential notes, because we had to discuss all these issues, and I did not ask these questions out of the blue. We have discussed all these matters. So we have a matter of principle, whether the confidential traffic between the client and the counsel can be disclosed to the Prosecution. It is definitely part of the confidential relationship between the client, and in that sense, it is privileged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. So even if we do bear in mind the difference between the notes prepared by Mr. Kvocka so that he can use them during his testimony and the notes, the little notes, little pieces of paper that are part of the communication between Defence counsel and Mr. Kvocka. I think that despite that difference, as regards the aide-memoire, that the Prosecutor has no right to see such notes, if we are talking about notes used in order to refresh his memory. So these are the aide-memoire notes. We will use that procedure. Let me repeat. So as regards the notes used by the witness in order to refresh his memory, we rule that the Prosecutor has no right of access to such notes. I even thought that the Defence would be agreeable to that, but if the Defence is not, I think that it is appropriate for the Chamber to decide that the Prosecutor will not have the right to see the notes used by the witness in order to refresh his memory. So that was our ruling. As regards the order of examination, I hope that that is clear, and I think that we can now have a short break. After the break, we will start with the testimony of Mr. Radic, and I hope that Judge Riad will be here with us again. Ms. Hollis, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would ask one point of clarification. Since you have indicated that the aide-memoire of a witness to refresh their recollection would not be subject to disclosure at least to us, would that ruling be the same for our witnesses if they use aide-memoires to refresh their recollection, that they would not be disclosable to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Hollis. We will explain the position. In principle, the situation will be the same. However, we have to bear in mind relevant circumstances and act according to the case, on a case-per-case basis. But principle will be the same, and it will apply in the same manner on both parties. So now we are going to have a 20-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Radic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now going to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down, Mr. Radic. Before we proceed with your testimony, I have to thank Mr. Kvocka for the testimony given by him. Thank you very much, Mr. Kvocka. To the attention of the public, I should like to remind you that the Defence has asked that the accused Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic be heard at the beginning of the trial. You are probably familiar with our Rules. Rule 85, I believe, gives the possibility for us to change the order of evidence, this is provided for in this Rule, including the possibility for the Chamber to decide otherwise as regards the order of examination, of course bearing in mind the relevant circumstances and the situation of the accused.
