So we thought, the Chamber thought, that it would be in the interest of justice to proceed like this and has decided that the accused be heard at the beginning of the trial. You have probably heard our ruling as regards the use of notes. We discussed the matter with Judge Riad before we resumed, and he agrees with us. Of course, the parties have to be very careful, and we have to know exactly whether we are talking about notes exchanged between the counsel and the accused or the notes used by the accused who is testifying in their defence. We are mindful of the necessity of good communication. The witnesses are the ones who have something to say here, not the Defence or the OTP. Furthermore, the witnesses have the obligation to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and we have to enable them to do that in the best possible way and we have to help them in doing so. Of course, we all have our own habits of communicating amongst each other, and we all have -- it is perfectly understandable sometimes -- problems with remembering things. So I think that the principle that we have adopted is the right one, we will stick to it, but of course we will always be mindful of the particular circumstances of witnesses, and if there is a need, we will allow the exchange of notes. As you can see, the Chamber is not imposing -- is not saying anything to the witnesses or to the parties as to how to behave, how to communicate. We all know that we have our own way of communicating. We, of course, want the witness to face the Chamber when he's speaking, but of course if there is a need to use notes, we will be mindful of that need. Mr. Radic, you are now going to answer questions that are going to be put to you by your lawyer, Mr. Fila, and you will also have a chance to answer questions of the Prosecutor and also questions of the Judges. We haven't yet mentioned that, but I have to remind you that the Judges will also have questions for witnesses after they have been questioned by the parties. So this was the order of examination. Let me just say that we appreciated the way Mr. Simic has conducted his examination. Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. Now I will give the floor to Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Before starting the examination of Mr. Radic, I would like to ask to pose the first question to Mr. Radic whether he's in agreement with what Mr. Kvocka has testified to, the geographic location of Omarska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, we have to be, of course, mindful of the communication here. I don't want to put you under any pressure, but wouldn't it be better for you to come to the other table. Maybe you can exchange places with your colleague, and it will be easier for you. I don't want to impose anything, but I think it would be much better for you to come to this table here, to exchange places with your co-counsel. This is maybe a better way to proceed, but it's really up to you. Mr. Usher, could you -- no, Mr. Fila, I was thinking of this table here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you comfortable here, Mr. Fila? Is it okay for you? Thank you. Very well then. Thank you very much for your cooperation. You may proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had asked -- I posed a question whether before starting with the examination of Mr. Radic and in order to expedite everything that Mr. Kvocka said about the political background, about the location of Omarska, about the organisation of the police force, of the political parties, should not be repeated. I think that we should go straight to his personal involvement in Omarska. So I think that we can all resolve in one sentence, that is, whether Mr. Radic is in agreement with everything that Mr. Kvocka had testified to, and I think it would tremendously speed up the role process. If that is acceptable, I would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, do you feel comfortable there, as far as you can?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question to you is: You have heard Mr. Kvocka's testimony four days plus. You heard him answer questions of his attorney, Mr. Simic. Do you have any objections to what he had testified to?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I have no objections, and I would accept everything because I think he really explained it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that case, I will go to ask you questions about your personal life. Would you please tell us where and when were you born, what were your parents, who they were, and details about your family?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: My name is Mladjo Radic. My parents were Rado and Zorka. I was born in 1952 in the village of Lamovita, as a tenth child of an impoverished family. I completed eight years of school. I am married with a wife and three children. I served my military duty in Sisak, and then I applied for the police. In 1972 I became a police officer, and then I stayed in that job until I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It went pretty fast. After your elementary school, after the completion of elementary school, did you work anywhere before you joined the police force?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. At 17, I started working in a company which, at that time, was called Sava, and it was in Bosanska Gradiska. I worked there for four months as an unskilled labourer. It was construction work, building the highway, Prijedor-Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. And then?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: After the company had done this job and after the earthquake in Banja Luka in 1969, I started working for a construction company which was called Tempo. It was from Zagreb. I was on a team, on masons, and I was working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you become involved with the police?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: In 1971, at 19, I went to serve my military duty, and upon completion of this duty, I came back to my company. At that time, there was an announcement. The police were looking for recruits. So I applied. Then I was sent to training in the municipality of Mkrska. I completed that training. After that, I was sent back to Prijedor, and I was assigned to a local police station in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would now like to tender Exhibit number DR1, which is our marking, which is Defence "R" for Radic, number 1. I have copies, and I would like to examine that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is going to be Exhibit D1/3, and D1/3A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, what did you say? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1/3. What does "3" stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It stands for Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is possible to distinguish between documents presented by Mr. Kvocka and documents presented by Mr. Radic. That's going to be possible; right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Kvocka will have number 1; and Mr. Kos will be number 2; Mr. Radic number 3; and, finally, Mr. Zigic number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Fila, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you saw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are asking that the microphone of Mr. Radic be lowered a little. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You see this letter from the Ministry of the Interior, from the Legal and Personnel Department, dated 21 October 1998. This is what you can see in the heading section. Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: This document represents my personal information and details my career with the Ministry of the Interior, as far as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to this document, were you a police officer in the Prijedor Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document certifies that I was a police officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How long were you in this station?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I was there between 1972 and 1984, working as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any rank or were you a regular patrolman?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I was simply a police officer, patrolman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any lower rank thank yours?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it was the lowest rank?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the lowest rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: After the corridor was opened and after the Ministry's functions had been integrated, the interior decision was issued number 09/3-120-11/466, dated 27 of October 1993, reassigning me to the duties of police officer at the Prijedor Public Security Station, Prijedor Police Station II, Omarska department, which was part of the Prijedor Public Security Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On 27 October 1993, after the period where you stand accused, you were still a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a further two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did you first receive any rank?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I was promoted for the first time in 1994, and that was the chief -- shift commander, when I was reassigned in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I was an experienced police officer by that time. I was almost at the end of my career, and there was an internal agreement that towards the end of a police officer's career, a police officer was usually promoted so that they would get better benefits.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you ever carry out the duties of shift commander as it is stated here?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I never carried out those duties. After the transfer to Prijedor, I worked as a driver of a police van, and I worked in a duty room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the vehicle that transports detainees and arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On 20 October 1995, you were confirmed in the rank of Senior Sergeant?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was also part of the agreement that I should get better benefits, because the benefits at the end of a regular patrolman's career are very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This document covers the period between 1 April 1992 and on. Before that date you were stationed in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is where I was, and I was on duty as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The last paragraph details your salary. Can you tell us something about your remuneration?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was symbolic. It was next to nothing. It was an equivalent of 5 to 10 German Marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to tender a set of documents. It's a bundle which details everything that Mr. Radic has just testified about, and this is DR2. This is the decision of his appointment as a police officer; then a further decision confirming his status as a police officer from 27 October 1993; then a decision appointing him the shift commander; and in 1995, a decision on the establishment of rank as a Senior Sergeant. Then there is a personnel questionnaire, and then DR7 is the decision on termination of the employment of Mr. Mladjo Radic and the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska. If there are no objections on the Prosecution side, I would like to tender them as a bundle. So that is DR1 through 7 basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any objections to this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Fila, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did this termination of employment come about? You said by mutual agreement.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Sometime in 1996, after I learned about my indictment by this Tribunal, at that time my superiors had reached such a decision, to remove us from our duties, and we were offered a termination. So whatever I said about my promotion, about my rank, about my benefits, all this had just fallen through, and I found myself where I am today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you heard my learned colleague Niemann in his opening statement, he mentioned a document which shows that you were awarded --

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Niemann pointed out that I was awarded, and he made it sound as if it was for the alleged crimes that I perpetrated. But this is what I have to say to that: During my career as a police officer, my salary was 5 to 10 German marks. My superiors decided in a meeting that several people should be awarded, and I was among those people, after 25 or 26 years of service, and the only reason was the fact that I had spent so much time working there, and my wife, who was unemployed, and my children. And I think I understood this to be social assistance rather than some kind of award, because the total amount awarded to me was only about 50 German marks, from which I was able to buy flour and oil and other foodstuffs for my family. I don't know how my superiors framed it, whether this was an incentive or an award, but what it amounted to in my mind was social assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time, was your wife employed?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No, she was unemployed at that time. She is not employed even to date. Only one of my sons is employed. He works as a police officer in Prijedor Police Station II. He's been working as a police officer there, he was trained by the ITPF in that area, and he is a student of law, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you like a drink?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This would conclude the personal aspects of Mr. Radic's testimony and life, and I would just like to move on straight to the counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the period detailed in the indictment, you worked as a police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, by definition, or whatever I did at the police was a kind of prevention, which was my presence in certain locations, such as restaurants or roads, traffic control, to see whether people were drinking and driving; then providing security to schools, banks; patrols in the field. As Mr. Kvocka explained, I was never a boss, I was always number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Within the description of your job, were there night duties?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were night duties, traffic control, all kinds of duties that fall within the ambit of police officer duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is a duty officer's duty?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, to be by the phone, to be by the radio transmitter, to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was your superior in 1992, during the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: In 1992, Mr. Zeljko Meakic was my commander at the Omarska police precinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During his evidence, Mr. Kvocka presented certain documents detailing how the Omarska camp or the investigation centre, however you want to call it, looked like. We'll just call it Omarska. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know about this complex? Did you know how it looked before?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In addition to you two, two other people are charged alongside you. Do you know these two individuals? And if you see them, can you describe them?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Kvocka from the police precinct where I worked for ten years as a police officer. We worked together in this police precinct. I met Mr. Kos as a civilian while he worked in Zagreb at that time, and then he became the -- worked in Omarska at the police station. And I never met Mr. Zigic until I arrived at the detention unit in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How would your typical working day look, in Omarska, that is? How did you first come into contact with Omarska? And I don't mean the mining complex, but what the indictment charges you with.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I think that for a while I was off duty, and the duty officer, I forget who the duty officer was, Ilija Prpos or someone else, but he told me that the schedule had been changed and that I was to report to duty at 1900 hours, at some kind of a centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us a date, the month and year when this happened?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: That was in 1992, because I arrived at this newly established centre on the 27th, 28th, 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What happened next? You learnt that you were supposed to go to a centre of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I lived right next to the police station, some 200 metres away. I got dressed, I put on my uniform, as usual, that day. I came in front of the Omarska police station, and I found 10 or 12 other people there, most of them reserve policemen whom I did not know, some of them I knew. And a van belonging to the Electro Prijveda Company was parked there, from Prijedor, and once again one of these reserve policemen on duty told us to get into the van, which we did, and we were taken off towards the administration building belonging to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you arrive at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: We arrived at the camp in the van that I mentioned. We went past the main gate and went down to the administration building, or the canteen, the restaurant, and at the level of the canteen, the van parked and all of us got out, the 15 of us or so who were in the van. Commander Meakic met us there and told us that a centre had been set up in which there were certain individuals from the Prijedor area, and that it was our task to ensure security and to prevent these individuals from escaping, and that the new arrivals should replace the people that had already been positioned around the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's permission, I should like to have Mr. Radic indicate on the model itself where these individuals were, the people that were already there, and to show us which positions he and his group took up. That will facilitate our work, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila, I shall do so, and the usher will help us, he will give the pointer to the witness. And if necessary, Mr. Radic, you can get up to show us the exact positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you're now going to show us where the van stopped, who told you to take up your positions, and who stood where at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: We came from the road which leads up to the canteen itself, and there is a wider space --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting but we have a problem with the microphone. Could Mr. Radic be given a microphone? Because the interpreters are having difficulties in following him. Thank you. Let's try again. I think that things will be better now.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we arrived at the front gate, from this side [indicates], and we reached this area here, this is a plateau [indicates], a wider space. The van stopped somewhere here [indicates], next to this restaurant. We got out. Zeljko Meakic stood here waiting for us, and he told us that we would be guards in the investigation centre from now on, that there were individuals in that centre from the Prijedor area and that it was our task to see that they did not escape, and that we would be replacing the people who had already stood guard in the camp. I stayed here [indicates], in front of this garage. This was the garage facility. And I think I replaced Rado Ritan, or somebody like that, I don't remember exactly. Next to me was Mirko Jokic, on this side, and the other side, over here, was Marmat; whether his name was Rajko or Zivko, I can't remember. Then there was Milenko, and so on around the centre. We replaced the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we say then that you made a circle around the whole compound?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, right round this, along this green surface and round the whole compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see any people being held in the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were people -- no, there were people in front here [indicates]. These other facilities were closed, but we were told that in these buildings, there were some people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say "we were told," who told you?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: The commander, Zeljko Meakic, told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did anybody else tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Only Meakic?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now explain to us how long you stood in that position and how your first day ended in the compound?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was nighttime when I arrived. As far as I can remember, it was from 7.00 p.m. to 7.00 a.m., and then we were off for 24 hours and would return to duty after that. When I came the second time, I was positioned as a guard here [indicates], in front of the garage once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who told you where to stand?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody told us anything. We had already had this routine. So I would take up my position, Mirko would be next to me; across the away from us, somebody else, Marmat and all the rest of us, because it was the third or fourth shift on that second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: During my stay, there were several shifts here. One or two, it's not important, I don't know how many I actually did, but one day Zeljko Meakic came up to me and told me, "Mr. Radic, you are going to be transferred to the duty office."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't think he would say "Mr. Radic" to you.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, no, he didn't address me as Mr. Radic. He just said, "Radic, you are going to work in the office from now on, where we have our radio transmitter and the local telephone, and you're going to do other tasks, or if need be, do the task of guard." I took up my pistol, I took up all my equipment, and followed him into the building and took up my position in the office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you lift the roof up off of the building on the model -- lift the roof up.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: You mean me?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. I'd like to ask the usher to remove the roof from the building. Thank you. Now, Mr. Radic, show us how you entered and where your duty office was.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I entered through this door here, and from there I took a right turn, up the steps to the first floor. There is another staircase here, and so I went up to the first floor this way, which brought me to this room here, and it said B5 on the door, B5. That is the office in which we had our duty office premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was in the room?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: In the room there were two tables. One was next to the window, and two other tables were placed in the L-position. I sat at this table. There was an UKT transmitter, a telephone, and at the two tables here, there were two typists typing out something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were these typists from the Omarska department or from somewhere else, those two typists, these two ladies?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: These two ladies would worked at the security centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did they get there?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: They came there together with the inspectors, the investigators. When they came to work, they went with them, and they worked in the office, typed out what they had to do, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were the other rooms on that floor?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Room B11, B10, and B9 were the investigating rooms, rooms for interviews, interviewing rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was interviewed there?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: The inspectors, investigators worked there and interviewed the individuals. This office, B3, also served the same purpose. In B4, I don't know whether anybody was interviewed there. There was a sort of loudspeaker there. In the room marked B1, and this B1 here, that room was used by the investigators and their bosses or chiefs or whatever, and they had some documents -- stored some documents there. They would have their meals there. So we didn't go into those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you came to that particular office, that is to say, Meakic told you to go into the office and take up your duties as a duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you stand guard anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a guard sometimes at this position here, near the Torine tower. All this is glass. This is a glass partition. It was very hot, and it was very difficult to work there for 12 hours because of the heat, but we had to. So from time to time, I would do guard duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there any where elsewhere you did guard duty or only those two points?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. Just in front of the garage, and over here, and worked in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As a duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you do as a duty officer? What was your job as a duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: I sat there all the time. If there were any calls, incoming calls -- of course everything was coded -- if somebody asked to speak to the commander, I would go and find the commander, tell him that he was wanted, that he was asked Sana 1 calling Sana 3, and so on. All this was coded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So Sana 1, 2 and 3, those were the codes. Codes for what?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, Sana 1, it was Vran 1 afterwards, but these were codes for Drljaca, Chief Drljaca. Sana 2 might be Jankovic; Sana 3, Milutin Cadjo; Sana 4 would be somebody else. So this was coded.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You heard Mr. Niemann's introductory statement and there was a video played, and an individual with a gun could be seen on the tape. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking about this part here, this area here, then that was me in my standard police uniform, with a gun in my hand, standing to attention at my guard post.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do the guards have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I think that the commander -- shift commanders have them. No. The shift commander does not have a gun in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something else. There seems to be a misunderstanding. Let me repeat. Do the shift commanders have guns when they are on duty on their shift, doing their shift?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: The shift commanders do not, and it is the guards that stand guard. The shift commanders do not stand guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the tape, we can also see the detainees. The Prosecutor did not bother to explain where the individual detainees were, but did you have any barbed wire in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. And I'd like to see that tape once again. Where I was standing guard, that is probably me. The people running to eat in the canteen, they were people from Omarska. The individual eating out of the plate was from Omarska, and the barbed wire and those thin people, emaciated people are quite certainly not from Omarska, nor was there a barbed wire in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have spent a considerable amount of time on duty. Did Meakic tell you why it was you who was on duty?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me directly why it was me, but I can only assume why it was. Perhaps because, as I say, I have been a policeman for many years, and he knows I know how to operate a radio transmitter. He knows I won't get the wrong frequency. I can work a telephone and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, let us go back to the fact that you said that you were a policeman for many years and well acquainted with police practice. When you spent your time in the centre, in the camp, when people arrived, the detainees, when they arrived, was there any procedure by which you escorted the detainees? Were there any records, lists of individuals, things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The standard procedure was the following: When somebody arrived, if I was on duty and if that individual was to be retained, then a note would be written down on his detention, the time of his detention would be noted, but nobody else wrote reports of this kind, notes of this kind, documents, or sign them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can we then conclude that these individuals had no certificates, signed certificates and decisions on their detention?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. This was just an ad hoc practice. They were just people brought in ad hoc and detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the course of your stay, that is, and the two posts that you held, as a duty officer and as a guard standing duty, did you have the authority to order anybody anything?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When I say "anybody," I mean your colleagues, policemen.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. No. I never ordered anybody anything. I never issued any orders of any kind. Through my whole lifetime I was an ordinary policeman and always followed orders from other people. Probably the reason was that I wasn't very well educated, so I could not advance in my service. I was just an ordinary policeman, police officer, and always followed orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us that you worked in shifts throughout your stay in the centre, 12-hour shifts and 24-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who determined where you were going to work when you came to do your shift?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't actually determined, but it was standard practice. People knew where their posts were. So we would be brought in by van, we would come out of the van, and we all knew which post to take up. I would go up to the office, carry on my duty there. When I was told to be a guard, I would be a guard, I would go on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But who told you where to go?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, the first time we arrived, Mr. Meakic informed us of this and explained everything, and then, of course, there was no reason to explain again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But if somebody were to tell you, "You're not going to work in the duty office today, you're going to do your guard duty," who would say that?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Meakic did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he do that regularly?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would do that regularly. He was regularly in charge of my schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I want to indicate to the Trial Chamber here today is the following: Was the procedure by which you came, took up your duties, replaced each other, stood guard, was it any different from standard practice and procedure practised by an organised police force, as I hope our police force was?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it was different, yes, because had people worked under normal conditions, they would all have had police uniforms, they would have to come to work well shaved and well turned out, but of course, now people came with beards. They had various symbols, insignia, different uniforms. They would have a camouflage uniform on top, civilian pants, blue uniforms, different coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you went to the Omarska police station, did the duty officer tell you -- did he have a schedule and tell you where to take up your posts?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. The duty officer would never tell --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm talking about Omarska, when you went to work at Omarksa?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. We would go in front of the Omarska police station, we would get into the combi van, and we would be brought to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. You are talking about when the centre was set up, but before the centre existed, when you would go to work in the morning, what did your daily routine look like in Omarska as opposed to your routine at the centre?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended. Under normal conditions, I would not have any long arms. I would get a patrol list. If I had to tour a terrain, I would know the villages that I had to patrol, where I had to be at each given time in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So did you write reports of this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, do you want Mr. Radic to remain standing or could he sit down now? Perhaps it would facilitate interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he can sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can hear him better if he resumes his seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is a good point for a pause or shall we go on until 2.30? Which do you prefer, Your Honour? Shall we make a pause here? Can I go on to 2.30 without a break? Because if I have a break, it will be difficult for me to get through all the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness is capable of continuing, then I think it would be advisable to work until 2.30. If that is all right with you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You -- the Prosecutor has given us some material about witnesses and so on. In the indictment, you are called the shift commander, referred to as "shift commander." Were you, in fact, a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know where this term "shift commander" comes from. Perhaps the detainees used the term. But I was never a shift commander, nor was I ever positioned as a shift commander, except in 1995 when I was to retire. Then they gave me this sort of chit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How can you explain to us, then, the fact that many of the Prosecution's witnesses speak about Krkan's shift, for example? Why do you think they refer to it as Krkan's shift?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I have already said that I have worked in the police force for many years, that I worked in the Ljubija region for 12 years, and passing through Prijedor, Kozarac, then I spent 10 years working in Omarska until the conflict broke out. Many people knew me by my nickname, Krkan. And now I'd like you to understand that particular situation, where my acquaintances found themselves in an unfavourable situation, closed up, and then I came there to stand guard, to provide security and these 20 young men whom I worked with, half of them I didn't even know their names, and they didn't know me, but with my appearance, some of them knew me. Perhaps 3 per cent of those on the pista knew me, and they said, "Here comes Krkan," and, "This is Krkan's shift." And I also think perhaps you, Mr. Fila, are better acquainted with this. When you went with me down there, nobody would say "Krkan's shift," they would say, "Mr. Fila's shift."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, luckily I wasn't there, otherwise I might be the accused here.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: May I add as well, that the people down there had never seen the president of the municipality nor secretary nor tactical groups nor cantons nor any of this business of regions, provinces, they just saw me as a policeman and thought me to be responsible for everything that was happening to them, just as in my detention unit, I am very angry with the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you told me that amongst the detainees, there were some of them who were your friends and acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us go back to the introductory statement made by the Prosecutor. They criticise you for the fact that you never wanted to assist anyone in any way. You did not, neither did any of the others help anybody. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that statement made by the Prosecutor. I can quote several examples where, as a man, I did help a certain number of individuals. But let me also say that when I could help them, I found it very difficult not to be able to help people, because I was somebody who, until yesterday, was in town, I would go to dances, to weddings, to celebrations, even to funerals, and suddenly people would expect to get a piece of bread from me. When I had a piece of bread, it was difficult for me to give it to one person and not to give it to the man next to him who might have been more hungry than the man who'd asked me for the piece of bread. On the other hand, when I did have a piece of bread or two pieces of bread, I could never throw the bread away because I knew that many people would be hungry. So I did give as much as I could to people to help them, either clandestinely or quite openly, and to hell with what would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does the name Milenko Brisovac mean anything to you? Hasim Hodzic is the next name. Zdravko Ivanovic. Do those names mean anything to you? Reza Hodzic, Idriz Mujikic, Milan Anusic, do those names mean anything to you? Were they detainees?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you help them?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Those are only some of the names of the people whom I helped in one way or another, and I did help many more people than the ones that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Idriz Mujikic, his nickname was Tazo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What ethnic group did these individuals belong to?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any hostile feelings towards the members of other religions and other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely no. In 1982, when I worked at the Omarska police station, I was the kum or best man to Stipe Pavlovic. And Mr. Kvocka, a few days ago, explained what the institution of kum means in the areas that we come from, and as he said, "God is in heaven; kum is on earth."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now show document DR14A, which was translated this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Stipe Pavlovic was a Muslim or Croat or Serb, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, is Stipe a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stipe is a Croat. His father's name was Pejo. We were good friends; we would visit each other, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Fila, but can we have the number of the document? I'd like to take advantage of this opportunity to ask the registrar to give us the numbers of the other documents tendered by Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. There were nine documents in all, and they were numbered D2/3 to D10/3, those were the documents in question, and the present document will be numbered D11/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Registrar, I think that we have to be able to identify documents properly. I think Mr. Fila has submitted DR2, 3, 5, 6, and 7. I don't see nine -- I can't see nine documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Fila said that it would be to D10.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, to D7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Then as far as I'm concerned, this document will be marked Exhibit D8/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And this document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it's this one, D8/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Radic, the one you're holding?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate whereby it is certified that Mladjo Radic, son of Rada, born in Lamovita, was present as a witness, that is, best man, at the wedding of Stipe Pavlovic and Olga Didovic on the 7th of January, 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What nationality is Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat. He comes from the area of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I apologise, but I don't think we have that document. You said that it has just arrived, that it came in this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It just came in. Mr. Registrar received it in 12 copies. It has been translated, of course. My marking is DR14A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have it Mr. Fila. Thank you very much. You may resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any other person acting in that capacity, as a best man, who was not of the same ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I used to work in the Ljubija police station with Mr. Ibrahim Denic who was of Muslim ethnic background. We are more or less of the same age and our wives went to school together in Prijedor, in secondary school. His wife is a shop assistant and my wife used to work in the catering business. So Mr. Denic was the godfather for my children. Let me clarify that a little bit. It was a new kind of relationship, new kind of capacity. I would often ask myself about the ethnic background of my children, for example. My eldest son is 25 and my youngest son is 13, and none of them were baptised according to the Serbian religious tradition, or Croatian Catholic religious tradition, and I didn't circumsise them either, of course as Muslims do, or Jews, so they're not that either. So we had this new type of ceremony after the birth of the child. The godfather has to cut a few hairs of the child, and I keep one lock of the hair and the godfather keeps the other, and the third lock is distributed among the hosts. This is the kind of ceremony that we adopted at that time. This happened in 1976. When my second son was born in 1978, his wife, Senada, was his godmother. She had to cut his hair during that ceremony. And when my third child was born, their daughter, Arijana, was the godmother, that is, she cut the hair of the child, for my third child.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your time at the centre, did anything happen to his son?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: While that was going on, I happened to be at home, and one day, around 2.00, 2.00 in the afternoon, I don't remember exactly, I received an anonymous telephone call. The person wanted to know whether it was the Radic residence, and I asked who it was, and the voice said, "It doesn't matter but you have to listen to me now." And the voice went on, saying that on the junction of the Omarska and Lamovita roads, halfway between Prijedor and Banja Luka, that my godson was lying on the ground. He was in a very confused state, and then the person hung up. So I wanted to verify that because the voice told me that I should do something about that person, to take him to the hospital. So I called the health centre, and it was an individual by the name of Rosic, a driver who answered, and I told him, I actually lied, I told him that a wounded child was lying near the junction in question and that the child should be transported to the Banja Luka hospital to get medical aid. So the person went there, and he actually transported the child to the hospital in Banja Luka. The child stayed there for a few days in hospital, and later on I learned that he had been playing near the house and had fallen off the third floor of his house, so that the child was unconscious and in such a state that he was transported to the hospital. So this woman, godmother, called me. She told me that she was there, and she told me that the child would stay there for a while. So I said that she should wait for me on the following day, near traffic lights in Banja Luka, near the hospital. So I went to Banja Luka by bus, the driver was Ratko Kobis, I took a bag full of food. My wife helped me pack that bag, and Senada, the woman in question, was really waiting for me. So I gave her the bag, I gave her some money, I don't know how much. So that child was taken there to hospital, and he's still alive. And when he left -- after he left the hospital, I would often go to Prijedor to see him. But the times were difficult, the transport wasn't really functioning. I had a son who was in school in Prijedor, and every Friday, my wife, if not every Friday, then every other Friday, my wife would pack a bag full of foodstuffs for him, so we would take that opportunity to take some food to that woman as well. She had one brother in Trnopolje, and apparently she took that food to him, but that bag somehow disappeared, so I never got it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What does the name Dragica Srdic tell you? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Dragica Srdic was my godmother's neighbour, and she was disseminating some kind of misinformation as to my being a guard there, and she used to work there as a cook as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be enough. We have mentioned your wife.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did it come about that she started working in Omarska? What exactly was it that she was doing?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, prior to the war, she used to work at the mine restaurant. After the break-out of the conflict, she stopped working, but she had a so-called work obligation. She had to report to the restaurant and start working. So she was in charge of preparing the food, together with about ten other cooks, and this is where the food was being prepared for the detainees, for the military, for the guards, and so on. It was a tremendous task but she didn't receive any money for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you in a position to release anyone from the camp, to let him go home?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No, sir. No, I wasn't. I was not in a position to release anyone, or to let anyone leave the investigation centre. That was simply not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You heard Mr. Kvocka's explanation as to the powers and the authority of the police station. Would you agree with the statement that the food situation -- that the food and water had nothing to do with your job description?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No, it had really nothing to do with us. We were simply providing guard duty, and we had nothing to do with food or water.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While your wife was working there, did she have any contacts with other women there, with female detainees?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did. Much to my surprise, one day when she came back from work, we sat together to have coffee, as we usually do, and she told me, "I heard some good things about you today, and I hope you will remain that way." So we joked a little about that, and I didn't know where the information had come from. I asked her whether she had been with Simo Drljaca or some other official, but she said no, she was actually talking to Suada Ramic, Mrs. Cikota, and one or two other female detainees in the camp. So I asked her, "Well, how did you come across them?" Because I knew that these women were detained there. She said that they had somehow come to the restaurant, that they were sitting in the restaurant, and they offered them some food. So they had some food there and coffee, and you know how women are, they started chatting. So my wife asked them about their accommodation, because she knew that there were some men there as well. She wanted to know whether they had any problems or similar. So Mrs. Suada said, "No, madam, on the contrary. We do not have any problems. We have our guard who is more of a guardian to us, Mr. Krkan, and we do not have any problems whatsoever because he's there." So at that moment these other women started laughing, including my wife. And Mr. Suada said, "Well, what are you laughing about? I did not say anything funny." Well, then other women told her that I was the husband of the lady they were having this conversation with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you know that you are charged with sexual assaults on female detainees. Is there any truth in that? You are under an oath, Mr. Radic. I'm reminding you of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to be honest as a man, and I have to say that there is no truth whatsoever in that statement. Of course I have read the indictment. Since we are talking about Mrs. Suada Ramic, I have to say here that after the close-down of the camp in 1992, I ran into her in Prijedor. She was with another lady. And because there had been some reports on TV that 60.000 people had been detained there, she wanted to know more about it. She wanted to know whether there had been any problems there. So we had this conversation, and she said that she had not had any problems there. When I arrived to the detention unit, I told that to the Prosecutor, and I can state that before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. Please do not go on. During your stay there, did you ever hit anyone? Did you ever kill anyone?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, no. I was there regardless of the circumstances. There were a lot of people there whom I knew from before, with whom I had grown up. So I often ask myself what I would expect from the people guarding them. I wanted to know how I would behave in their shoes. I concluded that I would probably expect from the guards to behave in a proper manner and not to do any harm. So I told myself, "Mr. Radic, you shall not kill. You do not have any reason to kill or to beat or to harm anyone in any way. You're not going to do that, because this is not human, this is not moral, and you always have to bear in mind how you would feel in their position."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you did say that you used to see people beaten up, with bruises, and that people had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. While on one occasion, which was going to the restaurant, I was actually standing behind the place from where the food was being brought in, and one of the female detainees who was distributing the food, I don't know which one, whether Mrs. Ciga, Mrs. Rajkovic -- they were the ones who worked most so I knew them best -- and they said that a guard had been beating someone on this lower part of the pista. So I turned around, and I went to this other entrance of the restaurant, and I indeed observed the guard by the name of Govedarica. There he had been beating that man. So I went to him and I told him, "Well, Zdravko, were are you doing this? There are hundreds of people here sitting on the pista, and you're beating this man here." So then he was very rude to me. I have to apologise here. He told me, "Well you can suck my cock." He told me that it was none of my business, and that I should go back to my place of duty, and that he knows perfectly well how to do his job. I must say here that I had no legal authority whatsoever to do anything. I did say that to him, and I wanted to tell him not to do it, because I felt it was not a thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you personally afraid for yourself in the centre?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not easy for me, especially after the incident which was related by Mr. Kvocka, the incidents in which a number of people were wounded. This was a very significant incident for all of us, because we didn't know what to do. I mean, we didn't know what to expect. We could expect a bullet in the back any time. So the situation was quite uncomfortable for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show a document which we managed to obtain. It's a duty roster marked as DR8. I apologise, the copy is not very well. So I should like Mr. Registrar to give the original copy to Mr. Radic, because the Registry has been supplied with the originals.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have photocopies here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original was given to Mr. Fourmy. It's a document concerning the shift. But I think we're all familiar with it. I will show this piece of paper to the witness and he will understand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember seeing it. I remember seeing the original, but here in the courtroom we have only photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we will use the photocopy to give some explanation, but the Chamber will dispose of the original as well in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we do have the original and a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit is marked as D9/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, could you tell us briefly what this document is all about?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Let me say this is a duty roster regarding the organisation of work while I was there in Omarska. This was kept at the Omarska police station. This concerns my schedule from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m., for example, but I don't see the dates here. Normally they should be legible as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. They are legible on the original. Could you please tell us whether this document shows how much time you spent in Omarska and when exactly you were there?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very accurate rendering of my schedule. You can see exactly when I worked, and you can also conclude, on the basis of this evidence, when I was absent from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you see other shifts as well?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. This concerns only me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who would replace you after your duty?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Well, these other people who were also guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the SDS political party?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show the document marked as DR9, and I would like to ask the accused to tell us more about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D10/3, and D10/3A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: This is a certificate whereby: "It is certified that Mr. Mladjo Radic, Milojica Kos, born in the village of Lamovita, Prijedor municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina, were not members of the Serbian Democratic Party as evident from the existing documentation of this municipal board. Dusan Beric."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you now please have a look at the document DR10 and document DR11 together.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document DR10 will be marked as Exhibit D11/3, and document DR11 will be marked as Exhibit D12/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, one can see from this documentation that you were a voluntary blood donor.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you tell us why you were a voluntary blood donor?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I have already stated that as a 19-year-old man, I did my military service, and while I was in Sisak, where my unit was quartered, my name was called, together with three other names, by a duty officer one morning. So we did not know what it was all about, but we were called to his office. They told us to sit down, which was a bit surprising for an officer to say that to a simple soldier. So he told us that he had seen our medical documentation from the recruitment, and he said that he found out that our blood type was 0-negative, and he asked us to give blood, because during the night, Mr. Ivan Puropak [phoen], the commander of my garrison, had had a serious traffic accident and that he was in hospital somewhere in Sisak. So I agreed to give blood. We went to the hospital in question to give blood. Our Captain spent some time in hospital. Later on he was discharged. I remember that I gave blood on one or two more occasions, which earned me two extra days of vacation. Later on, when I join the police and came back to my area, I thought that -- I realised that I was actually able to save somebody's life with this ability. So I joined the local association of blood donors, and I used to give blood during a certain period of time. I think I gave blood altogether 100 or 103 times, each time, 350 grams of blood. I think I gave altogether more than 35 litres of blood. For me, it was never an issue whether the individual in question was a Croat, Serbian, Gypsy, or Muslim. This was of no significance for me whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, were you involved in any military operation?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You learned about your indictment because it was a public one?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned about it in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you go in hiding after you learned about the indictment? Did you leave your place of residence? Did you abscond in any way?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: No. I went on with my normal life in Prijedor. I stayed in my apartment in the JNA Street, which was renamed in the meantime. My whereabouts were the usual ones. I would go to my weekend house in Lamovita. It's an old house. Not even my father remembers when it was constructed. I was informed as to the fact that I was hiding, but I have to say that I had no means whatsoever to hide, to change my identity, and it so happened that I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You had two identity cards when you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I had my proper identity card, and I also had my official police force identity card. After I retired, I was actually given that identity card by Mr. Drljaca. And he told me to hide, but I didn't hide. I took this other identity card, together with my regular one, put in my wallet, and I kept carrying it around. If I had any intention to go into hiding, I would only be carrying this other identity card.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, why didn't you surrender?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: Let me be perfectly honest, Mr. Fila. At the time the indictment against me was issued and during the time of Mr. Drljaca in the area of the Prijedor municipality and even beyond, I can claim, with full responsibility, that no person was able to resist anyone -- to resist the authority in any way, or Mr. Drljaca, for that matter. And I know that if I had surrendered, that it would probably have been to the detriment of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You will allow me, Your Honours, two more questions, please. Mr. Radic, you are aware of the inhumane treatment in Omarska. You know that there had been killings, and you yourself stated that conditions were not humane and that there had indeed been killings. But could you tell us here, how do you feel about that now and then? How do you feel about the fact that you yourself were part of it?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you. As a man, I can only say that I am ashamed of everything that happened there. I'm ashamed for the people who did what they did, and I do deplore the fact that those people suffered and went through all this ordeal, and I do feel humiliated. But I believe that because I personally did not harm anyone, did not kill anyone, did not steal anything from anyone, I believe that I am not guilty for those things. But as a man, I do feel ashamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why didn't you run away? Why didn't you throw away your uniform and simply flee?

utterances.speaker: MLADJO RADIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Fila, I would be signing a death sentence for my family had I done such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Thank you for being so efficient and brief. You may sit down. The Trial Chamber would like to thank you, Mr. Radic, for coming forth as a witness. The proceedings against you will continue after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Hollis, I should like to ask you now about the order. We were about to -- we actually had to start with your case on Monday, but there was a possibility for bringing a witness before that. You said that you would make some effort and try to find witnesses and start before Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Based on the changes in the schedule, last week we made arrangements to have witnesses here available to testify on Wednesday and Thursday, and those arrangements have been successful. So that we have definitely three witnesses to testify and we have three others who would be in a position to travel if they're told to do so, but that would be beginning on Wednesday, Your Honour, based on what we understand the schedule would be from last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me propose something. I do agree that we have some somehow changed the situation of the Prosecution, but I would like to suggest a change. We will not have enough, two days, for six witnesses, for obvious reasons. You will probably need Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday. Is it possible for us to reschedule the Status Conference and to have it tomorrow instead of Friday? Again, I apologise for trying to change the schedule, but this might not be such a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I also wanted to rethink the schedule for the Status Conference, but we do need certain time to review the work that has already been done, and before we make any conclusions, we have to see the Statutes of the proceedings, we have to see about the agreements of the parties, and see whether we are able to go even further in that respect. So we have to think carefully about that, see if there would be any consequences if we rescheduled the Status Conference. I don't know how the parties stand, what their position is, but in any case, I wanted to have that Status Conference maybe not right away but after a certain time, after we have had an opportunity to think about it. Ms. Hollis, do you have anything to say about the proposal given by Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We certainly appreciate Mr. Fila's attempts to expedite the proceedings. We share Your Honour's concern that perhaps if we had it tomorrow Your Honours would not have sufficient time to evaluate what has happened in order to form your own positions as to what the significance of that may be. However, should you decide you want to have a Status Conference tomorrow, certainly we would be able to participate in such a conference meaningfully, I believe. We also, Your Honour, have another issue that we wanted to raise before we began to put on your evidence, so if you'd like to hear that issue now, I'll go into that. Actually, two issues. If you'd like to hear that now, I'll put that on the record or else I can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me suggest something to both parties. If I have accurately understood, I think that the Prosecutor is agreeable as to Wednesday for witnesses, next Wednesday. We can have the Status Conference on Tuesday. We can deal with all the outstanding issues during the Status Conference, including possibly the issue of preliminary questions before the examination of witnesses, and on Wednesday, we can start with testimonies; that is, we can start with the Prosecution evidence. That way, we can have enough time to prepare for the Status Conference which will be held on Tuesday. We will be dealing with all the preliminary questions relating to the evidence, and then we start on Wednesday. I don't know whether this is possible or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's the translation or perhaps I'm just confused, but my understanding is this week is the last week we will sit in this two-week period and that next week Your Honours will be in another case. So if what you had proposed was that we begin testimony next week, that's not what we had in mind. When I said "Wednesday," Your Honour, I meant Wednesday of this week. Perhaps I misunderstood or perhaps I'm confused, but I think we're talking about this week in terms of whether we would put evidence on this week or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Ms. Hollis, and thank you very much, because sometimes we forget that we have double work here. So what you're suggesting is to bring witnesses this Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. When the schedule changed last week, in order to try to accommodate the change in schedule and not to unduly delay the proceedings, we went to the witnesses yet again and asked if they could accommodate what was now a fourth change in schedule. Based on witnesses who were most available to us, we were able to come up with three witnesses that we could definitely count on and three additional that perhaps we could bring if we needed them for this Wednesday, which would be the 7th, the 7th and 8th. It was our understanding that there would not be a session on the 9th. I'm sorry. Today is the 6th, tomorrow is the 7th. Wednesday the 8th, Thursday the 9th, those are the days we tried to arrange witness testimony for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we have a problem here. I think that we have been working for about one hour and forty-five minutes. We should normally have a break. The Chamber has other commitments aside from this case, as you know very well. Of course, we have to think about the interpreters. One hour and forty-five minutes is definitely too long. We had to finish at 2.30. What I can propose at this point is the following: We really have to prepare ourselves for this Status Conference. We have to analyse in depth the work that is before us. We have to think about the conclusions that we will reach. What I wanted to ask Ms. Hollis was, the questions, what are the questions that have to be treated right away and the problems that can be resolved? And in that case, we could start on Wednesday with the Prosecution evidence. So I will give you the floor, Ms. Hollis, so that you can tell us something about the issues that you want to discuss before calling your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One issue is a substantive issue. It has to do with the recent arrival at the detention centre of a co-accused for Omarska crimes cases -- excuse me, for Omarska camp crimes. The second one is a procedural matter that has to do with summaries we will use with our witnesses. Let me begin with the first matter, which is a substantive matter. Last night, a Mr. Prcac was transferred to the Tribunal from Bosnia-Herzegovina. He is a co-accused with these accused in crimes at Omarska. What the Prosecution would like to raise as an issue before you today is, in light of this fact, the issue about balancing certain rights and responsibilities. We suggest that the arrival of this man here at this time raises the need to balance the most efficient and fair use of judicial resources with the right of these accused to a fair and expeditious trial. In looking at that balance, we suggest that some thought, and significant thought, should be given by this Chamber to whether those needs could be balanced by an adjournment, a reasonable adjournment in these proceedings, of a reasonable time to allow Mr. Prcac to prepare his defence and to be joined to this trial. Mr. Prcac's trial will in virtually all respects, not all, but virtually all respects, parallel the evidence that will be brought forth in these proceedings. Given the time that these proceedings take, the traumatic impact on victims and witnesses who must appear here, we suggest that it would be -- there's a great interest in bringing Mr. Prcac into this case, if that can be done without depriving these accused of their right of a fair and expeditious trial. In trying to determine whether their interest would be violated, we suggest that these accused have been in confinement for a considerable period of time up until now, the Prosecution has not begun to put on its case in chief, and that if a reasonable delay were allowed, say, perhaps, a 90-day delay, to enable Mr. Prcac to be able to be joined with this trial, and I don't mean joined with the indictment because they are already joined in the indictment, but to have his trial occur with these accused, we suggest that that would be a proper balance of very significant interest. We certainly agree that the fundamental interest that must be protected is the right of all these accused to a fair trial and an expeditious trial, but we suggest that "expeditious" is defined not by a specific number of days or months but rather when looking at all the circumstances. So that is the issue that we want to raise because we believe that it is a significant issue and it is an issue of substance which must be decided before we begin our case in chief, we suggest. Would you like me to move to the procedural issue or would you like me to wait for a response to my first substantive issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you turn to the procedural issues, I would like to state that we take into account what you have said. We will think until tomorrow. We will take up the issue again tomorrow because we have to hear the evidence as well, and I don't think we have enough time for that today. So we will turn to your second issue so that we are at least informed about its contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The second issue, as I said, is a procedural issue and it has to do with how we are going to deal with the summaries that we will prepare for each of our witnesses which will cover much of the background that would otherwise have to be taken up by live testimony in the courtroom. If we do as at least one other case has done and we have the summary read aloud in the courtroom to the witness and have the witness adopt it, that certainly is one procedure, but that does take time in the courtroom. Another procedure, and one that we have been considering, is that when we speak with the witnesses before they testify, we have the summary read to them in their language, have them agree that each paragraph does reflect what happened to them, it is reflective of their experiences, it is accurate, and then when they came in to testify, we would ask them if, indeed, that procedure had been followed, and if the summary, which we will mark as a Prosecution Exhibit, does truly and accurately reflect information about them and their circumstances. We suggest that this procedure would save some time in the courtroom. Now, we have provided copies of these summaries to the Defence, we've provided them to them in English. They would be read to the witness but much the same way as would happen in the courtroom. So we would like the Court's guidance or direction, if you will, as to what they would prefer is our procedure with the summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. You may sit down. We will just take note of the following for the time being, because I may stand accused of mistreatment in the courtroom here. So I will just wind up with the following: We could perhaps go a little further, it's no longer the same issue, but when we have a document here in the courtroom, a document that is produced, we always want to hear the witness speak about the document. I would like you to consider the idea of separating documents, those who speak for themselves and the documents that need certain explanation by a witness. If we have a written document, it's sometimes very easy; we can all read the document, we don't need a witness to read it for us. So in order to expedite things, I think we can proceed in this manner. But I would like to close for today. Let me just remind you that there are three issues that need attention for the next time. We will start on Wednesday with Prosecution witnesses. However, before we start the examination of witnesses, we have to decide on certain procedural issues. The Status Conference that we have already mentioned will be used to reevaluate the agreements that have been reached, and next week, the next time, we will have -- we will finish this week, and then we have 15 days without Kvocka, and then after that we will have the Status Conference. I think that by that time, we will all be able to think about the issues and that we will then reassess the agreements that have already been reached, and we will know whether we are able or not to expand things after the examination of this witness. I cannot go any further at this point because I have already said, the interpreters are very tired. I'm afraid they're going to bring a class action against me, and I must not risk that happening. So we will finish for today. Thank you very much for your cooperation, and we will see each other again on Wednesday [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of March, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
